pos: n. (proper name; a son of David born in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elishua', God is salvation or God of riches, from 'el, God, and shua', salvation, wealth.
biblical_def: Elishua is one of the sons born to David after he took the throne in Jerusalem: “Ibhar also, and Elishua, and Nepheg, and Japhia” (2 Samuel 5:15). The Chronicler repeats him: “And Ibhar, and Elishua, and Elpalet” (1 Chronicles 14:5). In the list of 1 Chronicles 3:6 the King James text reads Elishama in his place, and the margin notes that this is Elishua; the second Elishama of that list is a different son. The sons of David's Jerusalem years are introduced with a sentence that carries a quiet judgment: “And David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron” (2 Samuel 5:13), which the law had forbidden the king. Elishua himself did nothing that Scripture records. His name, God is salvation, belongs to a household that would know rape, fratricide and rebellion, and from which, nevertheless, the LORD brought both the royal line through Solomon and, through Nathan, the line Luke traces to Christ.

corruption_summary: David's many wives are read as divine approval of royal polygamy; the law forbade the king to multiply wives, and Scripture records the cost.
corruption_paragraphs: Because God blessed David, some argue that his multiplied wives must have been blessed too. Deuteronomy 17 forbade the king to multiply wives to himself, lest his heart turn away, and the narrative of 2 Samuel shows a house torn by the rivalries his marriages created.

The principle to recover is that God's blessing on a man is not His endorsement of every act of the man. The line of promise ran through David's house by grace, in spite of its disorder, not because of it.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Bathsheba, son of Ahithophel)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eli'am, God of the people or my God is kinsman, from 'el, God, and 'am, people, kinsman.
biblical_def: Eliam is named twice. When David saw a woman from his roof, “one said, Is not this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, the wife of Uriah the Hittite?” (2 Samuel 11:3). And among David's mighty men stands “Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34). If, as most readers have concluded, these are the same man, the consequences are heavy. Bathsheba was the daughter of one of David's own thirty and the granddaughter of David's chief counsellor, and the king's sin struck at the house of men who had served him. That would explain much about Ahithophel, whose counsel “was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God” (2 Samuel 16:23) and who went over to Absalom when the son rose against the father. The Chronicler names Bathsheba's father Ammiel, the same two words reversed. Eliam himself is silent in the text; his presence is the reminder that sin against one woman was sin against a whole household.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern retellings often make David and Bathsheba a romance or a matter between two people. The text names her father and her husband before it names her, and both were men who served David.

The principle to recover is that sexual sin is never private. It wrongs a husband, a father, a household and a people, and its harvest in David's house, the sword that did not depart from it, began with a question about whose daughter she was.

pos: n. (proper name; one of David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eliqa', perhaps God has spewed out or God of the congregation; the meaning is uncertain.
biblical_def: Elika is one of David's mighty men: “Shammah the Harodite, Elika the Harodite” (2 Samuel 23:25). Two men from the same small town of Harod, near the spring where Gideon once sifted his three hundred, stood together in the thirty. In the Chronicler's parallel roll Elika's name does not appear, and Shammah is given as “Shammoth the Harorite” (1 Chronicles 11:27), so that Elika is known from one verse alone. The roll of the mighty men is Scripture's honour list for those who “strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10), and the mere presence of a name on it is a commendation. Elika did nothing the text records except stand with David when David was hunted and when he reigned. That was enough to have his name written.

pos: n. (proper name; Hezrai or Hezro the Carmelite, one of David's thirty)
biblical_def: Hezrai is one of David's mighty men from Carmel in Judah: “Hezrai the Carmelite, Paarai the Arbite” (2 Samuel 23:35). The Chronicler spells him Hezro: “Hezro the Carmelite, Naarai the son of Ezbai” (1 Chronicles 11:37). One man, two spellings, in two independent rolls. His town was the Carmel of the hill country of Judah, near Maon, the place where Nabal sheared his sheep and Abigail met David with bread and wine. A soldier from that district on David's roll is a small mark of how the outlaw years turned into a kingdom: the country that once held a churl who scorned David's men later sent one of its own to be counted among them.

pos: n. (proper name; Hiddai or Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, one of David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Hidday, perhaps joyful or shout; Chronicles has Churay, Hurai.
biblical_def: Hiddai is one of David's mighty men: “Benaiah the Pirathonite, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash” (2 Samuel 23:30). The Chronicler names the same man Hurai: “Hurai of the brooks of Gaash, Abiel the Arbathite” (1 Chronicles 11:32), and the King James margin notes the identity. The brooks or valleys of Gaash lay below mount Gaash in Ephraim, where Joshua was buried at Timnath-serah. A man of Ephraim among David's thirty is a sign that the king's strength was not drawn from Judah alone. The roll of the mighty men gathers soldiers from Bethlehem and Carmel in the south, from Benjamin, from Ephraim's hill country, and even from Ammon and Moab, and it does so to show that the kingdom given to David was for all Israel, as the Chronicler says, “according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10).

pos: n. (proper name; Hashem the Gizonite, father of men among David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Hashem, fat or shining; 2 Samuel has Yashen, Jashen. Not to be confused with ha-shem, the name, a later Jewish circumlocution for God.
biblical_def: Hashem appears in the Chronicler's roll of David's mighty men: “The sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite” (1 Chronicles 11:34). The parallel in Samuel reads, “Eliahba the Shaalbonite, of the sons of Jashen, Jonathan” (2 Samuel 23:32), and the King James margin notes that Hashem and Jashen are one. The phrase “the sons of” suggests that more than one of his sons served in the guard. Readers should not confuse this Hashem with the Hebrew expression ha-shem, the name, which later Jewish usage employs in place of the divine name; the Gizonite's name is a different word, and the coincidence of English spelling is only that. Hashem is known for one thing: he raised sons who stood with David.

pos: n. (proper name; Hothan the Aroerite, father of two of David's mighty men)
biblical_def: Hothan is named in the Chronicler's extended roll of David's mighty men: “Uzzia the Ashterathite, Shama and Jehiel the sons of Hothan the Aroerite” (1 Chronicles 11:44). His town was Aroer, very likely the Aroer on the Arnon east of Jordan, “on the bank of the river Arnon” (Joshua 13:16), in the territory of Reuben, which places this father and his two sons among the Transjordan men who joined David. The Chronicler's roll runs longer than Samuel's precisely in these eastern names, and the extension records how widely David drew his support. Hothan's name means a seal, and he is sealed into the record not by his own deeds but by his sons'. Two brothers from one household in the thirty is a family's whole loyalty given to the LORD's anointed.

pos: n. (proper name; father of two of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elna'am, God is pleasantness, from 'el, God, and na'am, to be pleasant, delightful.
biblical_def: Elnaam is named in the Chronicler's roll of the mighty men: “Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite” (1 Chronicles 11:46). His sons Jeribai and Joshaviah served in the guard. The verse that holds his name also holds Ithmah the Moabite, a foreigner from a people the law shut out of the congregation “to their tenth generation” (Deuteronomy 23:3), now standing in the honour guard of the king whose great-grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess. Elnaam's name, God is pleasantness, uses the root of Naomi's name, the pleasant one who called herself Mara in her bitterness. The juxtaposition is a small picture of David's house: built of Israelites and foreigners, of the bitter and the pleasant, all gathered under the LORD's anointed.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a house whose sons served David)
etymology: Hebrew Chakmoni, wise, from chakam, to be wise; the gentilic is Hachmonite.
biblical_def: Hachmoni is the head of a house that gave David two of his notable servants. The chief of the mighty men is introduced as “Jashobeam, an Hachmonite, the chief of the captains” (1 Chronicles 11:11), and the margin renders it “son of Hachmoni”. Among David's officers of state, “Jonathan David's uncle was a counsellor, a wise man, and a scribe: and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni was with the king's sons” (1 Chronicles 27:32). Whether Hachmoni was one man or the founder of a family, the house produced both a warrior who lifted his spear against three hundred at once and a tutor or companion trusted with the king's children. The name itself means wise, and it is fitting that it stands in the verse that sets a counsellor and a scribe beside the man appointed to the royal sons. David's kingdom was defended by the spear and ordered by wisdom, and the house of Hachmoni supplied both.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite harper at the bringing up of the ark)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eliphlehu, God distinguish him or God of his distinction, from 'el, God, and palah, to separate, distinguish.
biblical_def: Elipheleh is a Levite of the second degree appointed when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem. “David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick” (1 Chronicles 15:16), and Elipheleh is listed among their brethren, a porter, and then among the harpers: “And Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, and Azaziah, with harps on the Sheminith to excel” (1 Chronicles 15:21). Sheminith appears to be a musical term, perhaps an octave or an eight-stringed instrument, and it reappears in the titles of Psalms 6 and 12. The context is the second, lawful attempt to move the ark, after Uzza died for touching it on a cart. This time the Levites carried it, as the law required, and the worship that accompanied it was ordered, appointed and skilled. Elipheleh is one of the names by which Scripture shows that worship in God's house was neither improvised nor unregulated.

corruption_summary: Worship is treated as spontaneous self-expression; David's ark procession was appointed, ordered and led by named Levites under God's law.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern worship culture often prizes spontaneity and treats structure as quenching the Spirit. The bringing up of the ark came after a fatal lesson at Perez-uzza: God would be worshipped as He commanded, by the persons He appointed, in the manner He required.

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship. David's Levites sang with joy, but their joy was ordered; every harper and porter had his appointment, and the whole was done according to the word of the LORD.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Eliphlehu, God distinguish him; a Levite porter and harper at the ark's coming to Jerusalem.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Eliphlehu, from 'el, God, and palah, to distinguish.
A Levite of the second degree (1 Chronicles 15:18).
A porter, and a harper on the Sheminith (1 Chronicles 15:21).
Appointed when the ark came up from the house of Obededom.
Sheminith recurs in the titles of Psalms 6 and 12.
